posts.title: Tuning before the doors open
posts.excerpt: Ninety minutes before every concert the hall belongs to one person and a tuning fork.
posts.content:
Shun Morioka arrives at four. The heating has been on since noon, because a piano tuned in a cold room drifts as the audience warms it.

He tunes from the middle outwards, listening for the slow beats between strings. By half past five the lid is up and the room is quiet again.

posts.title: Why we rarely use microphones
posts.excerpt: A small timber room carries a voice to the back row without help. Here is when we still reach for a microphone.
posts.content:
The hall was tuned for unamplified sound: strings, piano, voices, a jazz trio played with brushes. In most concerts nothing goes through a speaker.

For a quintet with drums we draw the curtains behind the balcony, which shortens the reverberation, and sometimes lift the bass a little. Never more than that.

posts.title: A quartet that never pauses
posts.excerpt: Yui Asaka on why the Aster Quartet plays whole quartets without stopping between movements.
posts.content:
Applause between movements is lovely, she says, but the silence after a slow movement is part of the piece. So the quartet asks the audience to hold it.

Their October concert is three late quartets with one interval. The stubs say seventy minutes; she thinks it will feel shorter.

posts.title: The bass without an amplifier
posts.excerpt: Teodor Lind has played double bass in clubs for thirty years. Neiro Hall is one of the few rooms where he unplugs.
posts.content:
In a club the bass is felt more than heard. Here you hear the wood, he says: the scrape of the string, the thump of the body.

He leads the Low Strings on 19 December, two basses, a cello and a voice, the last concert of the year.

posts.title: Records on the foyer shelf
posts.excerpt: The listening shelf in the foyer changes with every season. This autumn it holds records by the artists on the programme.
posts.content:
There is a turntable, a pair of small speakers and a short stack of records. Before a concert you can play one side.

Most of the records were made by artists who have played here; some were recorded in the hall itself, on a quiet Monday.

posts.title: A cello sonata in the making
posts.excerpt: Hana Ellery is writing a new piece for the Tessellate Duo. She tried the first page in the empty hall.
posts.content:
Composing for a room is different from composing for a page, she says. The low notes here bloom, so the piano part became lighter.

The piece will be premiered on 11 December, between two sonatas the duo has played for years.
